scenes.text: A female common frog releases eggs into pond water while a male releases sperm close by. Now look at a hen's egg in a nest. In this example, it is already fertilised. Both eggs are outside the body when we see them. But did sperm and egg join in the same place? To answer, we need to follow the reproductive event, rather than classify an animal from where its egg ends up.

Recall from the previous lesson that sperm and egg are reproductive cells called gametes. Each carries inherited information in DNA. When a sperm joins an egg, we call that fertilisation. It can begin the development of a new animal. In this common-frog example, the female's eggs are already in the pond when sperm reaches them. The joining happens in water outside her body. That makes it external fertilisation. External describes the joining place, not whether the parents live in water.

Why release the gametes close together? A sperm must reach an egg before it can join it. Nearby release shortens that journey. The water keeps these exposed gametes from drying out and provides liquid in which sperm can swim. But water alone does not guarantee a meeting. A current can carry sperm away from the eggs. If the two types of gamete are not present at the same time, they may miss each other too. So a suitable watery setting, a nearby release and overlapping timing support fertilisation in this case.

The hen uses a different route. Sperm is transferred into the female during mating. Inside her body, it can reach an egg near the beginning of a tube called the oviduct, the passage that carries the egg onwards. Joining there is internal fertilisation. The moist reproductive tract reduces the gametes' exposure to drying, which is useful on land. That protection does not remove the need for sperm to enter the female and reach an egg. The location gives a useful advantage under dry conditions. It does not promise that every egg will be fertilised or that an offspring will survive.

Return to the egg in our opening nest. In a hen, sperm reaches the egg before the hard shell is added. The egg then passes along the reproductive tract, the shell forms around it, and the hen lays it. In our supplied fertilised egg, the joining has already happened inside the body. Later development can continue in the laid egg when conditions support it. For this bird, remember the order: join, shell, lay. That order explains why an egg in a nest does not make fertilisation external. Find the joining place first.

Try a changed condition. Two groups of common frogs release the same numbers of eggs and sperm into pond water at the same time. Their gametes remain able to fertilise for the same length of time. In group B, a stronger current carries sperm away from the egg patch. Classify the fertilisation in this route. Predict how B's opportunities for sperm to reach eggs compare with group A, and explain why. Then name one result these observations cannot tell us. Pause here to decide.

The fertilisation is external because sperm and egg join in pond water outside the female. For B, the stronger current carries sperm away from the eggs, so sperm has fewer opportunities to reach them in the stated comparison. Equal starting numbers do not remove that extra separation. The unchanged viable lifetime, the time gametes remain able to fertilise, does not remove it either. We cannot calculate an exact number of fertilised eggs from these observations. Nor can we predict how many young will survive and later reproduce. The evidence supports a change in meeting opportunities, rather than a guaranteed offspring count.

We used two animal examples to locate fertilisation and explain a relevant advantage. Common frogs join gametes outside in water. Our hen joins them inside before shell formation and laying. Different routes still depend on suitable conditions. Next, we'll follow how a flower produces a seed. Detailed mammalian reproduction comes later.
